I found a wallet in a shopping cart at Walmart last Tuesday. Brown leather. Worn soft at the edges. Tucked under one of those reusable bags someone had left behind.

I almost didn't see it. I was returning my cart because that's what I do — I'm the person who walks it back to the corral instead of leaving it in the middle of the parking lot like an animal. My husband makes fun of me for it. Says I'm the last honest person in America. I tell him somebody has to be.

The wallet was light. No credit cards. No debit card. Just a driver's license and $400 in cash. Twenty-dollar bills, folded tight, held together with a rubber band. The kind of cash someone counted carefully before they left the house.

The license showed a woman's face. Small. White hair. Born 1947. The photo was old — she looked younger in it than the birth date suggested. The address was on Route 4, a town I'd heard of but never been to.

I pulled it up on my phone. Thirty-one minutes away.

I stood there in the Walmart parking lot holding this woman's wallet and I had a conversation with myself that I'm not proud of. Thirty-one minutes is a long drive. I could turn it in to customer service. They'd probably call her. She'd probably come back and get it. Probably.

But $400 in cash with no cards means this woman doesn't have a bank account. Or doesn't trust them. Or can't get one. And if she comes back to Walmart looking for this wallet and it's gone — even if it's sitting behind the customer service desk — she's going to spend the whole drive home believing she'll never see that money again.

I know what that feels like. Not the money part — the part where you lose something and the not-knowing eats you alive. The hours between losing it and finding out if it's okay. I wouldn't want someone to put me through that if they could prevent it.

Plus I had nothing else to do. It was Tuesday. My day off. I'd come to Walmart for laundry detergent and garbage bags. Not exactly a packed schedule.

I got in my car and drove.

The GPS took me off the highway after twenty minutes onto a two-lane road that got narrower the farther I went. Past a dollar store. Past a church with a gravel parking lot. Past a farm stand that was closed for the season.

The house was small. White. Set back from the road with a chain-link fence and a yard that was neat but tired — the kind of yard someone used to take care of and still tries to but can't quite keep up with anymore. There was a garden bed along the front with stakes in it but nothing growing. A birdbath that was dry. A truck in the driveway that hadn't moved in a while — you could tell because the leaves had settled around the tires and nobody had swept them.

I sat in my car for a minute. Looked at the house. Looked at the wallet. If I'd known what was waiting on the other side of that door — not just a woman, but a story that would change my life — I'd have sat there a little longer. Gathered myself. But I didn't know. So I just walked up and knocked.

It took a while. I heard movement inside — slow, careful steps. A chain lock sliding. The door opened about four inches and a face appeared in the gap. Small. White hair, just like the license. But older now. Thinner. Eyes that were sharp but tired.

"Can I help you?"

"Ma'am, my name is Janet. I found this in a shopping cart at Walmart." I held up the wallet. "I think it's yours."

She looked at it. Then at me. Then back at the wallet.

She opened the door all the way. Her hands were shaking when she took it. She opened it immediately — didn't check the license, didn't check anything else — went straight for the cash. Counted it. All twenties. All there.

Then she pressed the wallet against her chest with both hands and closed her eyes.

"Oh thank God."

"Is it all there?"

"Every penny." Her voice broke on the second word. "Every penny."

She looked at me. Her eyes were wet.

"This is for my husband's headstone. Eight months he's been in the ground without a name on it. I've been paying it off forty, sixty dollars at a time. Cash. I drive to the monument company on Route 11 every month and hand them whatever I can. This was the last payment. Four hundred dollars. I took it out of my savings jar this morning and put it in my wallet and drove to Walmart to get a few things before I went to make the final payment."

Her voice steadied, then broke again.

"His grave has been unmarked for eight months. Every time I go visit him I'm standing in front of a flat patch of grass that could be anyone. There's no name. No dates. Nothing that says he was here. That he was real. That he mattered."

"This money was going to fix that. Today. And then I got home and the wallet was gone and I thought — I thought he was going to stay invisible."

She tried to hand me a twenty.

"No ma'am. I don't want your money."

"Please. You drove all the way out here."

"I'll tell you what. If you've got coffee, I'll take a cup. It's a long drive back."

She smiled. First time. And it change …

My husband started taking a statin in June of last year.

Took his 40mg Lipitor every morning at 7 sharp.

Took the fish oil pills he ordered off the internet.

Cancelled his Friday night steak at the place we'd gone to for thirty years.

Quit eggs entirely.

Went on the Mediterranean diet.

Walked three miles a day.

Started eating oatmeal every morning, of all things.

He did everything the doctor told him.

He died of a massive heart attack on October 25th at 5:23 in the morning.

He was 61 years old.

His cast-iron skillet is still hanging above the stove.

I can't take it down.

If I take it down, he's really gone.

His pill organizer is still on the windowsill above the sink.

I can't empty it.

The Sunday slot is empty.

He took that Sunday pill at 7, the way he always did.

He never made it to the Monday slot.

Monday through Saturday are still full.

Six doses of the Lipitor that was supposed to save him.

If I empty it, he's really gone.

I need to tell you what happened to Roy.

Because I keep seeing the same posts I was making a few months before he died.

"My husband's doctor just put him on a statin, any tips to bring his cholesterol down naturally?"

And it makes me physically ill.

If you're over 50 and your cholesterol is high, or someone you love's is, please read this whole thing.

I know it's long.

I know you're scrolling.

I know you have things to do.

A year ago I would have given anything, everything, for someone to sit me down and tell me what I'm about to tell you.

Roy went in for routine bloodwork last June.

He felt fine.

Better than fine.

He was sixty.

He still hunted every November.

He still rebuilt the engine in his old truck on Saturdays.

He thought he was indestructible, and honestly, so did I.

Two days later the doctor called.

LDL of 187.

Total cholesterol of 264.

"Your LDL is very high, Roy. We need to talk about your diet. And I'm putting you on a statin today."

Roy was quiet on the call.

I was in the kitchen pretending not to listen.

"How much red meat do you eat?"

"Steak a couple nights a week. Bacon and eggs on Sundays. Maybe a ribeye when we go out."

"That's enough to do this. You need to cut out the red meat and the eggs, completely, no exceptions. I'm putting you on 40 milligrams of atorvastatin. One pill every morning. We'll retest in three months."

Roy hung up and sat at the kitchen table for forty minutes without saying a word.

Then he stood up, walked out to the garage, and emptied the chest freezer.

I watched him bag up a ninety-dollar ribeye he'd been saving for our anniversary.

A tomahawk from the butcher.

A New York strip.

Two coolers of venison from his November hunt.

The whole freezer, loaded into the bed of his truck and driven down to the food bank, gone in under an hour.

"That's it," he said. "I'm done."

And he was.

He picked up the Lipitor from the pharmacy that afternoon.

Took the first pill at 7 the next morning with a glass of water.

Set the bottle on the windowsill where he'd see it every day.

I bought him a Sunday-through-Saturday organizer and started filling it every weekend.

Two weeks in, our neighbor told him over the fence that his own cardiologist had him on fish oil for his cholesterol.

Roy ordered a bottle off Amazon that night and added it to the organizer the next Sunday.

For a hundred and three days, he didn't touch a bite of red meat.

He didn't miss a single pill.

No steak.

No bacon.

No eggs.

Not at his nephew's wedding in August.

Not at the football game in September.

Not at his own 61st birthday dinner in October, where his brother ordered the porterhouse right in front of him and Roy ate the grilled chicken breast.

I threw out thirty-eight years of recipes.

I learned to cook things I'd never made in my life.

Lentil stew.

Baked fish.

Bowls of grain and kale I couldn't have named a year before.

I'd stand at the stove at six watching him push the food around his plate, and I'd pretend it was fine.

I ate the same dinners he did.

If he had to give up everything he loved, I wasn't going to sit across from him with a ribeye on my plate.

He stopped going to the neighbor's Wednesday cookouts because he couldn't sit there with a side salad while everyone else ate steak.

I stopped going too.

His oldest friend told him he was no fun anymore and stopped calling.

He skipped the deer trip to the cabin with his brother for the first time in thirty years.

He gave up a piece of himself he'd been carrying his whole life.

And he did it anyway.

Because the doctor said to.

Then his legs started aching at night.

A deep, bone-tired ache that wouldn't go no matter how he stretched.

I'd lie next to him listening to him shift from one side to the other, trying to find a position that didn't hurt.

He was tired, and sleep never touched it.

Asleep in his chair before the news was over.

Taking the stairs one at a time, gripping the banister and pulling himself up, and I'd remember the man who used to tak …

rows.body: This year Endeavour Early Education Kariong celebrated #ScienceWeek with baby chicks provided by Henny Penny Hatching! The children were able to watch the chicks hatch from eggs in their own classroom, and witness them grow over two weeks as we all loved and cared for them. This experience helped teach the children empathy and responsibility, and opened up conversations about lifecycles and farming. This was an enriching experience for children, parents, and educators alike and brought lots of joy to all of us over the last two weeks!

The delivery driver left it on my porch by mistake.

A brown-paper package, hand-addressed in careful blue pen, the corners taped down the way people used to wrap things before everything came in a plastic bag with a barcode.

The name on it wasn't mine.

The street wasn't mine either.

Three roads over from ours, one of those little lanes that dead-ends at the creek.

I could have set it back out for the driver to sort out the next day.

But it was going to rain that afternoon, the kind that comes in sideways off the fields and doesn't let up till dark.

And the handwriting on it was the careful kind, the kind somebody sat down and took their time over.

So I walked it over before the weather turned.

A woman about my age answered the door with a dish towel over her shoulder, and her whole face changed the second she saw the writing.

"That's from our daughter in Oregon," she said. "She still wraps them the way her grandmother used to. Nobody wraps a thing anymore."

She held it against her chest for a moment like it was the girl herself standing on the porch.

Then she wouldn't hear of me leaving without a cup of coffee.

That's how it works out here, or how it used to, before everybody quit answering their doors.

Her kitchen smelled like coffee and something baking, and there were grandkids' drawings taped to the refrigerator, going yellow and curling at the corners.

Her husband was at the table with the newspaper folded to the crossword, and he started to get up to shake my hand, and I watched his grip give out.

Just for a second.

His fingers closed around my hand and then let go before he wanted them to, and he set his coffee down harder than he meant to, some of it going over the rim onto the saucer.

He laughed it off.

"Getting old," he said. "Can't hold onto anything anymore. Used to be able to crack a walnut in this hand."

His name was Walter.

He'd been a machinist for thirty-nine years, he told me, proud of it, made parts you could measure to the width of a hair.

Half the porch rails and mailbox posts on that street he'd set himself, and he could still tell you which ones and what year.

He told me about the parts he used to turn on the lathe, pieces that went into engines and machines all over the county, cut to a tolerance you measured with a gauge that cost more than his first car.

He was proud of it, and he had every right to be.

His wife stood at the counter refilling my cup and watching him the way you watch someone when you're frightened for them and working hard not to let it show.

He reached for the sugar and knocked the spoon clean off the saucer, and he laughed, and she laughed with him, and neither laugh got anywhere near their eyes.

I didn't understand yet what I was looking at.

I only knew the kitchen was warm and the coffee was good and something underneath all of it was badly wrong.

Hands like a vise his whole life.

And now he couldn't keep hold of a coffee mug.

His wife walked me back out to the porch when I left, and she stood there a minute in the doorway the way people do when they've been carrying something alone and a stranger feels safer to hand it to than family.

She told me she was worried about him.

His legs ached at night so badly he couldn't lie still.

She'd hear him get up and move to the recliner, and still not settle, and be back up an hour later.

He was tired, and no amount of sleep seemed to touch it.

He fell asleep in his chair before the evening news was half over now, a man who used to be up before the birds and out in the shop by six.

One morning she'd found him sitting at the bottom of the porch steps, just resting, because his legs wouldn't carry him back up and he didn't want to call out for her and worry her.

He'd stopped going out to the shop entirely, she said, the shop that had been the center of his whole life.

He'd quit driving to the diner for his Saturday breakfast because his hands shook too much for him to trust himself with the wheel.

The dog walks had gotten shorter and shorter until some days he only made the end of the driveway and turned back.

She kept finding him sitting down in the middle of things.

On the edge of the bed.

On the bottom porch step.

On the bench out in the garden, just gathering himself to stand back up.

He was 64.

Her own father had still been splitting firewood at 80.

The doctor had looked him over and said it was his age.

Said it was probably the blood pressure, or all the walking, or just the years arriving all at once the way they do.

The only thing the doctor had ever changed, she said, was to start him on a pill for his cholesterol that spring.

I stood on that porch with the first drops of rain starting on the roof, and I felt something cold go straight through me.

Because my own husband is 63.

And six weeks earlier his doctor had put him on the exact same pill Walter was taking.

A statin.

I hadn't thought a single thing of it.

The doctor said his cholesterol had crept up, wrote  …

Three roads over from ours, one of those little lanes that dead-ends at the creek.

I could have set it back out for the driver to sort out the next day.

But it was going to rain that afternoon, the kind that comes in sideways off the fields and doesn't let up till dark.

And the handwriting on it was the careful kind, the kind somebody sat down and took their time over.

So I walked it over before the weather turned.

A woman about my age answered the door with a dish towel over her shoulder, and her whole face changed the second she saw the writing.

"That's from our daughter in Oregon," she said. "She still wraps them the way her grandmother used to. Nobody wraps a thing anymore."

She held it against her chest for a moment like it was the girl herself standing on the porch.

Then she wouldn't hear of me leaving without a cup of coffee.

That's how it works out here, or how it used to, before everybody quit answering their doors.

Her kitchen smelled like coffee and something baking, and there were grandkids' drawings taped to the refrigerator, going yellow and curling at the corners.

Her husband was at the table with the newspaper folded to the crossword, and he started to get up to shake my hand, and I watched his grip give out.

Just for a second.

His fingers closed around my hand and then let go before he wanted them to, and he set his coffee down harder than he meant to, some of it going over the rim onto the saucer.

He laughed it off.

"Getting old," he said. "Can't hold onto anything anymore. Used to be able to crack a walnut in this hand."

His name was Walter.

He'd been a machinist for thirty-nine years, he told me, proud of it, made parts you could measure to the width of a hair.

Half the porch rails and mailbox posts on that street he'd set himself, and he could still tell you which ones and what year.

He told me about the parts he used to turn on the lathe, pieces that went into engines and machines all over the county, cut to a tolerance you measured with a gauge that cost more than his first car.

He was proud of it, and he had every right to be.

His wife stood at the counter refilling my cup and watching him the way you watch someone when you're frightened for them and working hard not to let it show.

He reached for the sugar and knocked the spoon clean off the saucer, and he laughed, and she laughed with him, and neither laugh got anywhere near their eyes.

I didn't understand yet what I was looking at.

I only knew the kitchen was warm and the coffee was good and something underneath all of it was badly wrong.

Hands like a vise his whole life.

And now he couldn't keep hold of a coffee mug.

His wife walked me back out to the porch when I left, and she stood there a minute in the doorway the way people do when they've been carrying something alone and a stranger feels safer to hand it to than family.

She told me she was worried about him.

His legs ached at night so badly he couldn't lie still.

She'd hear him get up and move to the recliner, and still not settle, and be back up an hour later.

He was tired, and no amount of sleep seemed to touch it.

He fell asleep in his chair before the evening news was half over now, a man who used to be up before the birds and out in the shop by six.

One morning she'd found him sitting at the bottom of the porch steps, just resting, because his legs wouldn't carry him back up and he didn't want to call out for her and worry her.

He'd stopped going out to the shop entirely, she said, the shop that had been the center of his whole life.

He'd quit driving to the diner for his Saturday breakfast because his hands shook too much for him to trust himself with the wheel.

The dog walks had gotten shorter and shorter until some days he only made the end of the driveway and turned back.

She kept finding him sitting down in the middle of things.

On the edge of the bed.

On the bottom porch step.

On the bench out in the garden, just gathering himself to stand back up.

He was 64.

Her own father had still been splitting firewood at 80.

The doctor had looked him over and said it was his age.

Said it was probably the blood pressure, or all the walking, or just the years arriving all at once the way they do.

The only thing the doctor had ever changed, she said, was to start him on a pill for his cholesterol that spring.

I stood on that porch with the first drops of rain starting on the roof, and I felt something cold go straight through me.

Because my own husband is 63.

And six weeks earlier his doctor had put him on the exact same pill Walter was taking.

A statin.

I hadn't thought a single thing of it.

The doctor said his cholesterol had crept up, wrote  …

Don't waste your money on grounding sheets until you see what it did for my 94-year-old patient.

Look, I'm a doctor with three decades in public health, 

And I’ve constantly had patients come to me with joint pain…

But it was only when one of my patients who I play tennis with (she’s 94) couldn’t hit a forehand anymore that I was moved enough to try a grounding sheet for the first time.

I’ve seen her try all types of joint pills, but she was just not getting better…

Sometimes little progress. But not significant enough.

And she wasn’t the only one.

Hundreds of patients came to my clinic complaining about the same thing.

“I have Arthritis Dr… do I need surgery?”

But here’s where it gets interesting…

When patients came to me with joint pain, most of the time they did not have “arthritis.”

What they had was chronic inflammation.

Now, most people think inflammation means you hurt your ankle. It gets big, red, and sore.

But what I'm talking about is inflammation that’s happening inside the joints.

And this appears more for older people.

What happens is every day, your body gets damaged. From stress, bad air, processed food, and just living life.

This damage creates things called free radicals. 

Think of them like rust inside your body.

When you're young, your body cleans up this "rust" easily.

But as you get older, your body can't clean it up fast enough.

So the "rust" builds up and builds up.

Your body sees this buildup and sends inflammation to try to fix it.

But since new "rust" keeps forming faster than your body can clean it, the inflammation never stops.

That's chronic inflammation.

Some people get it worse because:
- Their genes make them bad at cleaning up the "rust"
- They have lots of stress in their life
- They don't sleep well
- They eat processed food
- They’re next to electronics all the time

This kind of inflammation is what I see behind joint pain, and even things like heart disease.

Now, if inflammation is the real culprit behind all these health problems, 

Then I know that not enough grounding is the cause of inflammation.

Because when your body is grounded… 

You CAN’T have inflammation.

I learned this when I was helping my 90 y.o patient who could barely move in the morning.

Her joints were so stiff and painful. 

When I first heard about grounding, I thought it wouldn’t hurt her, but it likely won’t help her either.

So I gave her a grounding sheet and had her sleep on it for just one night.

The next week, she was moving around like normal. 

Her morning stiffness was completely gone, and she could play tennis again.

In all my years as a doctor, I have never seen anything work like that.

She's 94 now. She cleans her own house, does everything for herself, and plays tennis 5-6 times a week.

Even my patients who’ve been told by other Doctors to do surgery have tried this sheet,

Within the first week, they told me they didn’t want to do surgery anymore.

Now… what is grounding?

It’s when you're walking barefoot on the earth’s ground,

Where all that dirty electricity from your phone, WiFi, and electronics gets balanced out by the earth's natural charge.

Your body voltage drops to zero the moment you step on the ground.

But here's the thing - you don't need to walk around barefoot all day to get these benefits.

One of the easiest ways to ground is while you sleep.

Just two weeks of sleeping on a "grounding sheet" could help you restore blood flow, clear out inflammation, improve circulation in your joints, boost energy, relieve pain and stiffness, lower cortisol, and best of all, help you sleep like a baby again.

Now the only grounding sheet I recommend to my patients comes from a company called “GroundingWell”, and here’s why:

The fabric has to be woven with real silver fiber. Silver conducts electricity from the earth to your body. 

Most companies use fake silver or barely any silver at all. 

And they do this to make more money. 

Some don't even include the cord you need to plug it in to have a pathway between you and the earth in the first place.

But GroundingWell uses 5% of pure silver threading on their sheets, and they include everything you need.

On top of that, GroundingWell comes with a 100% risk-free money-back guarantee for 90 days. 

And that’s because it's already been proven to work for 10,000+ people who are dealing with various pains and sleep issues.

Before I wrote this, I called GroundingWell. I told them I was going to share what I'm seeing with chronic inflammation.

They were so moved, they wanted to help more people who are suffering.

So they set up a special link where, instead of getting a GroundingWell sheet for their typical price of $199.00,

You can now get it for HALF the price.

But it gets even better.

GroundingWell knows that when one person gets the sheet, they usually want to help their spouse or family, too. So for a short time, they're including a FREE grounding mat (worth $69) with every sheet.
